theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Pointer Arithmetic and Heap Memory

Pointer arithmetic can be scaled only because every pointer type carries the size of its target. For T *p, the expression p + i is computed as the address in p plus i × sizeof(T) bytes, and p[i] is simply *(p + i). Subtraction runs the same rule backwards: the byte gap between two pointers is divided by sizeof(T), so q − p counts elements, not bytes. These results are guaranteed only while both pointers stay inside one array or at the address just past its last element; forming any other address, even without dereferencing it, is undefined behaviour.

theoryAdd.plainText: byte gap from p to q = (q − p) × sizeof(T), where q − p is counted in elements

items: p = realloc(p, n) leaks the old block when realloc fails, because the only pointer to it is overwritten with NULL; assign to a temporary and copy it back only on success.
realloc(NULL, n) behaves exactly like malloc(n), and free(NULL) does nothing, so both are safe starting and ending points.
Writing malloc(n * sizeof *p) instead of naming the type keeps the size correct if the declaration of p changes later.
To let a function change which block the caller's pointer refers to, pass the pointer's address (int **); a plain int * parameter changes only a copy.
Relational tests (<, >) are defined only for pointers into the same array; == and != may compare any two valid pointers, or a pointer with NULL.
After free(p) the address left in p is stale; setting p = NULL makes an accidental second free harmless and keeps a later if (p) test honest.

theoryAdd.text: NULL, '\0' and 0 are different ideas that share the value zero. NULL is a null pointer constant meant for pointers, '\0' is the null character (a char of value 0) that ends every string, and 0 is an ordinary integer. Use each in its own context: p = NULL, s[i] == '\0', n = 0.

For address questions, multiply before adding: new address = old address + n × sizeof(T). For pointer differences, divide the byte gap by sizeof(T). Always check whether the question wants elements (q − p) or bytes ((char *)q − (char *)p).

questions.questionText: After the declaration int *p, q; which statement is correct?
options: p is a pointer to int and q is a plain int
p and q are both pointers to int
p and q are both plain ints
q is a pointer to int and p is a plain int
questions.explanation: In a declaration the * belongs to each individual declarator, not to the type, so only p is a pointer. Write int *p, *q; to declare two pointers.
*p = *q copies b's value into a, so a = 7. q = p then makes q point to a as well, so *q = 10 overwrites a while b keeps 7.

questions.questionText: Given int x; int *p = &x; which declaration lets pp store the address of p (pp = &p)?
questions.explanation: &p has type int **, so pp must be a pointer to a pointer to int. int *pp[2] is an array of two int pointers, int (*pp)[2] is a pointer to an array of two ints, and int &pp is not valid C.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the null pointer in C is correct?
options: Dereferencing NULL always gives 0, because NULL points to address 0
free(NULL) crashes the program, so it must always be guarded with an if
NULL may be assigned only to pointers of type void *
A null pointer compares equal to 0 (and to NULL), and dereferencing it is undefined behaviour
questions.explanation: NULL is a null pointer constant that may be assigned to any pointer type and compares equal to 0; it points to no object, so dereferencing it is undefined behaviour. free(NULL) is defined to do nothing.

questions.questionText: Why does standard C reject the expression v + 1 when v is declared as void *v?
options: A void pointer can only ever hold NULL
A void pointer cannot store the address of an int or a double
The size of the pointed-to object is unknown, so the step cannot be scaled
A void pointer is read-only and cannot change after initialisation
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic moves by sizeof(*p) bytes, and void has no size. Cast first, for example (char *)v + 1 or (int *)v + 1; GCC and Clang accept void * arithmetic only as an extension that steps 1 byte.

questions.questionText:
The fragment below is compiled as C. Which numbered line causes a compile error?

int x = 5;
void *v = &x;         /* line 1 */
int *p = v;           /* line 2 */
printf("%d", *v);     /* line 3 */
printf("%d", *p);     /* line 4 */
questions.explanation: A void * cannot be dereferenced, because the type of the object it points to is unknown. Lines 1 and 2 are legal in C, since void * converts implicitly to and from any object pointer type (C++ would need a cast on line 2).

options: Compile error: a void * cannot be reassigned to an int address
Compile error: *(int *)v * 2 multiplies a pointer by 2
questions.explanation: A void * may hold any object address, and after a cast to the right type *(double *)v reads 2.5 and *(int *)v reads 7. Unary * binds tighter than binary *, so the second expression is 7 * 2 = 14.
**pp is x, so x becomes 15. *pp = &y changes p itself to point to y, so **pp *= 2 doubles y to 40, and *p now reads y, which is 40.

options: Compile error: NULL cannot be passed to a function
questions.explanation: The pointer q is passed by value, so alloc changes only its local copy p; q stays NULL and the new block is leaked. To change the caller's pointer, pass &q to a parameter of type int **.

options: The program crashes because a is still NULL
questions.explanation: grow receives &a, so *pp = malloc(...) stores the new address in main's a. The block holds 0, 3, 6, 9, so a[1] + a[3] = 3 + 9 = 12 and a[2] = 6.
*pp = q stores y's address in p, so (**pp)++ raises y to 10 and x stays 5. After pp = &q, **pp is y again, and y += x gives 10 + 5 = 15.

questions.questionText: Assume char is 1 byte, int is 4 bytes and double is 8 bytes. The pointers char *c, int *i and double *d all hold the address 1000. Which addresses do c + 3, i + 3 and d + 3 hold?
questions.explanation: Adding n to a pointer adds n × sizeof(pointed-to type) bytes: 1000 + 3 × 1 = 1003, 1000 + 3 × 4 = 1012 and 1000 + 3 × 8 = 1024.

questions.questionText: On a 64-bit system where pointers are 8 bytes, how do sizeof(char *) and sizeof(double *) compare?
options: They depend on the value stored in each pointer
questions.explanation: Both are addresses of the same width, so sizeof(char *) = sizeof(double *) = 8 bytes. The values 1 and 8 are sizeof(char) and sizeof(double), the sizes of the pointed-to types.
q − p counts int elements: 5 − 1 = 4. Casting both to char * makes each step 1 byte, so the same gap measures 4 × 4 = 16 bytes.
*p++ yields a[0] = 10 and then moves p to a[1]. (*p)++ yields the old value 20 and increments a[1] to 21, while p stays where it is.
*++p first moves p to a[1] and reads 15. ++*p then increments the value a[1] to 16 and yields 16; p still points to a[1], so *p is 16.
p[-2] means *(p − 2), which is a[2] = 5; a negative subscript is legal while the result stays inside the array. *(p − 4) is a[0] = 1 and p[-1] is a[3] = 7, so the sum is 8.
sizeof d is the whole array, 4 × 8 = 32 bytes. sizeof p is a pointer (8), sizeof *p a double (8) and sizeof *q an int (4); sizeof does not evaluate *q, so the null pointer is never dereferenced.
sizeof x / sizeof *p = 20 / 4 = 5 elements. p + 1 is still an int *, so its size is 8 bytes, and (p + 4) − (p + 1) = 3 elements, not 12 bytes.

questions.questionText: p and q are int pointers into the same array and n is an int. Which expression is NOT valid C?
questions.explanation: Adding two addresses has no meaning, so p + q is a compile error. An integer may be added to a pointer, and two pointers into the same array may be subtracted (giving elements) or compared.
The loop pairs 2 − 12, 4 − 10 and 6 − 8, adding −10, −6 and −2, so s = −18. After three passes p points to a[3] and q to a[2], so p < q fails and p − a = 3.
Before each test the (p, q) positions are (0, 7), (2, 6), (4, 5) and then (6, 4), which ends the loop, so the body runs 3 times. Only addresses are compared; the array values are never read.
't' is at index 4 of "pointer", so the loop stops with p = s + 4 and p − s = 4. *(p − 2) is s[2], which is 'i'.

questions.questionText: In C, what is the type of the result of subtracting two pointers that point into the same array?
options: ptrdiff_t, a signed integer type defined in <stddef.h>
The same pointer type as the two operands
questions.explanation: The difference is a count of elements that may be negative (p − q when p comes first), so its type is the signed type ptrdiff_t. It is printed with %td.

questions.questionText: Which pointer comparison is always well defined in standard C?
options: p == NULL, where p is any valid pointer
p < q, where p and q point into two unrelated arrays
p + 10 > p, where p points to the first element of int a[5]
p != q, where p is an uninitialised pointer
questions.explanation: Testing a valid pointer against NULL with == or != is always allowed. Relational operators are defined only for pointers into the same array (or one past its end), forming p + 10 beyond a 5-element array is undefined, and an uninitialised pointer must not even be read.

questions.questionText: In the declaration int *const p = &x; what is constant?
options: The value *p: it cannot be changed, but p can point elsewhere
The pointer p itself: it cannot be made to point elsewhere, but *p can be changed
Nothing: const in this position is ignored
questions.explanation: Read the declaration right to left: p is a const pointer to int. p = &y is a compile error, while *p = 5 is allowed.
const int *p protects the pointee, so *p = 5 is illegal but p may move. int *const q fixes the pointer, so q = &y is illegal but *q = 5 is fine.

questions.questionText: Given int x = 1, y = 2; const int *const r = &x; which statement compiles?
questions.explanation: r is a constant pointer to a constant int, so neither r nor *r may be modified. Reading through r is always allowed, which gives z = 1 + 2 = 3.

options: Compile error: s points to const data and cannot be moved
questions.explanation: const char * makes the characters read-only but lets the pointer move, so s += 3 points to "NTER". *(s + 1) is 'T', and 'T' + 1 is 'U' when printed with %c.

questions.questionText: After which fragment is p a dangling pointer?
options: int x = 4; int *p = &x;   /* x still in scope */
questions.explanation: free releases the block but leaves the old address in p, so p now dangles. Setting p = NULL after free removes the danger, and a null pointer or a pointer to a live variable is not dangling.

questions.questionText: Inside a function, the statements int *p; *p = 10; are executed. Which description is correct?
options: p is a null pointer, so the statement safely does nothing
p is a wild (uninitialised) pointer, and writing through it is undefined behaviour
p is a void pointer, so the statement is a compile error
p is a dangling pointer to freed memory, where 10 is stored safely
questions.explanation: A local pointer that is never initialised holds an indeterminate address, and storing through it may corrupt memory or crash the program. Initialise every pointer to a valid address or to NULL.

questions.questionText: Which fragment is free of undefined behaviour?
options: int *p = malloc(sizeof *p); free(p); p = NULL; free(p);
questions.explanation: After p = NULL, the second free(p) is defined to do nothing. Freeing the same block twice, freeing a variable that was never allocated on the heap, and freeing an address that is not the start of an allocated block are all undefined behaviour.

questions.questionText: Which call allocates space for 10 ints and sets every byte of it to zero?
questions.explanation: calloc(count, size) allocates count × size bytes and zero-fills them. malloc and realloc leave new bytes uninitialised, and malloc(10) requests only 10 bytes.

questions.questionText: What does malloc return when it cannot allocate the requested memory?
options: The address of the largest free block that is available
Nothing, because it waits until enough memory becomes free
questions.explanation: malloc, calloc and realloc report failure by returning NULL, which is why the result should be checked before it is used.

questions.questionText: Which standard C header declares malloc, calloc, realloc and free?
questions.explanation: The heap functions are declared in <stdlib.h>. <malloc.h> is a non-standard header found on some compilers and should not be relied on.

questions.questionText: p points to a block obtained from malloc. What is the risk in the statement p = realloc(p, 1000 * sizeof(int));?
options: realloc always frees the old block first, so its contents are lost
realloc can only shrink a block, never enlarge it
realloc expects a count of elements, so the size requested is 4 times too large
If realloc fails it returns NULL, p is overwritten and the original block is leaked
questions.explanation: On failure realloc returns NULL but leaves the old block allocated, so assigning the result straight to p loses the only pointer to it. Use a temporary: t = realloc(p, n); if (t != NULL) p = t;

questions.questionText: Which statement about realloc is correct?
options: realloc always returns the same address it was given
realloc sets the newly added bytes to zero
realloc may be used to resize a local array such as int a[10]
questions.explanation: Called with a null pointer, realloc simply allocates n bytes. When it enlarges a block it may move it to a new address, the added bytes are not initialised, and it works only on blocks from malloc, calloc or realloc.
calloc zero-fills the block, so the elements are 0, 0, 4, 0 and 12, and their sum is 16. With malloc instead, the untouched elements would be indeterminate.

options: An unpredictable value, because realloc discards the old contents
questions.explanation: The first loop stores 1, 2, 4 and 8 (1 << i), and realloc keeps them. Then p[4] = 8 + 4 = 12 and p[5] = 12 − 1 = 11, so s = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 12 + 11 = 38.
The second assignment overwrites the only pointer to the first 40-byte block, so that block can never be freed. free(p) releases only the 80-byte block, leaving 40 bytes leaked.

questions.questionText: Assume int is 4 bytes. The array int a[10] starts at address 4000, and int *p = &a[2], *q = &a[7];. What are the address held by p + 3 and the value of q - p?
questions.explanation: p holds 4000 + 2 × 4 = 4008, so p + 3 holds 4008 + 3 × 4 = 4020. q − p counts elements: 7 − 2 = 5, which is the 20-byte gap divided by 4.
m is an array of 3 row pointers, and row i holds i + 1 ints with m[i][j] = i + j. The diagonal gives 0 + 2 + 4 = 6, and m[2][0] = 2 + 0 = 2.
Swapping p and q exchanges only the addresses: p now points to b and q to a. *p = *p * 10 therefore changes b to 20, while a keeps 1.
